lead: A data bus is a shared set of wires and rules that carries digital words between avionics units. It replaces bundles of point-to-point wires with a defined word format, timing and error check. ARINC 429 is the civil one-way bus; MIL-STD-1553B is the military command/response bus. Both are still found in aircraft and helicopters, often beside newer Ethernet. This chapter shows how each word is built, how fast it moves, and why direction and topology change the design.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2, LRUs and IMA, for what an LRU is and why units exchange data.

blocks.text: ARINC 429 is a one-way serial bus used on civil aircraft. One transmitter drives a twisted pair, and up to 20 receivers listen. The pair carries a balanced differential signal: one wire goes positive while the other goes negative, and the receiver reads the difference. This rejects common-mode noise from nearby cables and motors.

Every transmission is a 32-bit word. Bits 1–8 are the label, an octal code that names the parameter. Bits 9–10 are the SDI, the source/destination identifier, used when two similar units send the same label. Bits 11–29 carry the data. Bits 30–31 are the SSM, the sign/status/matrix, which says whether the data is valid, No Computed Data, a test value, or a sign. Bit 32 is odd parity over the other 31 bits.

blocks.where: T_word is one word time in seconds; n is the word length in bits (32 for ARINC 429); R is the bit rate in bits per second.

blocks.text: ARINC 429 has two standard speeds: high speed at 100 kbps and low speed at 12.5 kbps. The bus is simple, deterministic and well understood. Its weakness is wiring: each direction needs its own pair, because a 429 pair has only one transmitter. One pair can carry many parameters as a stream of labelled words; a dedicated transmitter is a design choice made when a parameter needs a high, independent update rate.

MIL-STD-1553B is a bidirectional serial bus used on military aircraft, helicopters and spacecraft. It runs at 1 Mbps and uses Manchester II encoding: each bit is a low-to-high or high-to-low transition in the middle of the bit period. The transition carries the clock, so no separate clock wire is needed.

A 1553B word is 20 bits: 3 sync bits, 16 information bits and 1 parity bit. There are three word types. A command word comes from the bus controller and gives the remote terminal address, transmit/receive bit, subaddress and word count. A data word carries 16 data bits. A status word comes back from the remote terminal and reports address, message error, busy, subsystem flag and terminal flag.

One bus controller controls all traffic; up to 31 remote terminals answer. The controller sends a command, the addressed terminal replies with status, data moves, and a final status may confirm. 1553B is usually dual redundant: two independent buses, A and B, so one cable or transceiver failure does not stop the exchange. The controller decides which bus is active.

ARINC 429 suits civil systems that send many separate parameters from one unit to many listeners: air data computers to displays, inertial reference units to flight management, radio altimeters to warning computers. It is one-way, so a reply needs a second 429 channel. 1553B suits military systems that need many units on one shared bus and need confirmation that a command was received. It is command/response, not a free-running broadcast.

blocks.text: Modern civil aircraft add switched Ethernet such as AFDX for higher bandwidth; see Chapter 4.8. ARINC 429 and 1553B remain common because they are simple, proven and easy to certify or qualify.

examples.question: An ARINC 429 transmitter runs at 100 kbps and sends a 32-bit word. A MIL-STD-1553B bus runs at 1 Mbps and sends a 20-bit word. Find each word time. For a 1553B transmit message (remote terminal to controller) with one command, one data and one status word, find total time ignoring gaps.
steps: A transmit message is command + status + data words, so count = 1 command + 1 status + 1 data = 3 words. Tmsg = 3 × 20 µs = 60 µs.
A receive message would be command + status + data + final status, so the same one data word would give 4 words = 80 µs.
examples.answer: ARINC 429 word time is 0.32 ms; MIL-STD-1553B word time is 20 µs, and the three-word transmit message takes 60 µs ignoring gaps.
examples.check:
r1 = 100000
n1 = 32
t1_ms = n1 / r1 * 1000
r2 = 1000000
n2 = 20
t2_us = n2 / r2 * 1e6
tmsg_us = 3 * t2_us
print(t1_ms)
print(t2_us)
print(tmsg_us)

traps: ARINC 429 is one-way. Reversing the same pair does not make a reply channel.
1553B is command/response. It is not a free-running broadcast; a remote terminal speaks only when commanded.
Do not count the 1553B word as 16 bits when finding word time; the line word is 20 bits, of which 16 are data.
ARINC 429 label is 8 bits and parity is 1 bit; the data field is 19 bits, not 32.
Manchester II carries its own clock; a separate clock wire is not part of 1553B.
A 1553B transmit message is command + status + n data words. A receive message adds a final status word, so the same data costs one more word.

quiz.q: How many bits are in an ARINC 429 word, and what are the two standard bit rates?
quiz.a: 32 bits; high speed 100 kbps and low speed 12.5 kbps.

quiz.q: Why does an ARINC 429 reply need a separate channel?
quiz.a: ARINC 429 is one-way; the transmitter pair only sends from one source to receivers, so the other unit needs its own transmitter pair.

quiz.q: An ARINC 429 low-speed channel sends a 32-bit word at 12.5 kbps. Find the word time.
20 parameters must go from LRU A to LRU B, and 20 must come back from B to A. Compare the wiring of ARINC 429 with one 1553B bus.
quiz.a: 429 needs one transmitter pair per direction per transmitter, so 20 pairs each way if every parameter gets its own transmitter; fewer pairs if many labelled words are multiplexed on shared pairs. 1553B uses one shared bus (two cables if dual redundant) plus a bus controller; all 40 transfers share 1 Mbps and each costs command and status overhead.

quiz.q: Name the three MIL-STD-1553B word types.
Describe the command/response sequence for a 1553B receive message.
quiz.a: Controller sends a receive command; RT sends status; controller sends data word(s); RT sends final status.

quiz.q: A 1553B transmit message (RT to controller) has one command, four data and one status word. Each word is 20 µs. Find total time ignoring gaps. How much does the same data take as a receive message?
quiz.a: Transmit: 1 command + 1 status + 4 data = 6 words × 20 µs = 120 µs. Receive: command + status + 4 data + final status = 7 words × 20 µs = 140 µs.

quiz.q: Why is dual redundancy useful on 1553B?
quiz.a: A cable or transceiver fault on bus A can be bypassed by using bus B; the controller can retry, so a single failure does not stop communication.

beyond: Not for the exam. ARINC 429 is still designed into small civil units, while 1553B continues in military upgrades and spacecraft. Newer civil architectures move to AFDX (ARINC 664) switched Ethernet, covered in Chapter 4.8. Search for ARINC 429 word format, 1553B command word, and dual redundant bus.
